Program_Info.Program_Change_Info: Move is the button InstallerClean leads with in this version. It puts the unneeded files in a backup folder you choose, so you can satisfy yourself your programs still update and uninstall as normal before you delete that folder yourself, and putting the files back into C:\Windows\Installer restores everything. Delete is permanent: files no longer go to the Recycle Bin, the button and the confirmation both say so, and /d on the command line does the same. The scan does about a third less work on each file, which matters on the very large folders people report: on a folder of 800,000 files the memory it churns through drops from 2.4 GB to 827 MB, while offering an identical list of files. InstallerClean now has a written privacy policy setting out every time it touches the network or writes anything down, from the version check when it starts to the report you can choose to send, along with the crash log and the settings, neither of which leaves the machine. Eleven languages now use the words their own Windows uses, ninety changes checked against Microsoft's published terminology, and the command-line tool's help fits an 80-column window in every language.
Program_Info.Program_System_Requirements: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit). Administrator rights required to access C:\Windows\Installer.

English.Char_Desc_250: InstallerClean scans C:\Windows\Installer for MSI and MSP files, asks Windows Installer what is still needed and reads the same records out of the registry as well. Move what it finds to a folder of your choice, or delete it. Open source, Apache 2.0.

English.Char_Desc_2000:
C:\Windows\Installer is a hidden folder that fills up as you install and update software. Windows keeps a copy of each installer, and of each patch, so it can update or remove that software later. When a newer patch replaces an older one, both stay, and so do the installers of software uninstalled long ago. On machines with heavy MSI-based software such as Adobe Acrobat, Office or large dev tools, the folder can reach tens of gigabytes.
InstallerClean scans the folder and asks Windows Installer what it still holds a record of, then reads the same records out of the registry as a second source. It offers a file only when nothing installed on the machine claims it, or a newer patch has replaced it and no program could go back to the old one. Where it cannot get a straight answer, it holds the file back.
Delete is permanent. The files do not go to the Recycle Bin, and nothing is deleted until you confirm. Move puts them in a folder you choose instead, which lets you satisfy yourself that nothing has broken before you delete anything. Both are refused while Windows Installer has a transaction running or suspended.
The app reads the folder and the Windows records; it does not change your installed programs. On launch it asks GitHub once whether a newer version exists, which you can turn off in About. No ads, no telemetry, nothing running in the background.
A separate console executable, installerclean-cli.exe, ships in the setup build and as a standalone download, for scheduled tasks and unattended use, with its own exit codes and Windows event-log entries for scripting.
Sixteen languages across the app, the installer and the command-line tool. Setup and portable builds are both self-contained and need no .NET runtime installed.
Inspired by PatchCleaner, which does a similar job but is closed source and hasn't been updated since March 2016.
